records.symptom: A port repeatedly goes down and up (link flap).
signatures: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface <name>, changed state to down
records.meaning: The interface changed link state; repeated pairs of these messages for one interface within a short window indicate flapping.
likely_causes: Bad, unsupported or nonstandard cabling.
Unsupported, wrong or faulty SFP/SFP+ transceivers.
Loose connections or faulty patch-panel connections.
Bad or old endpoint devices.
Duplex or negotiation mismatches.
Bad switch port or module port.
Mismatched FEC settings (both sides must match).
alternative_causes: Endpoint sleep or power-save behavior (the document notes this may be expected).
Known bugs named by the document: CSCvu13029, CSCvt50788, CSCvu92432 (mGig interoperability/flaps) and CSCve65787 (autonegotiation for 100G/40G/25G copper).
diagnostic_steps: Confirm repeated up/down events on one interface and capture timestamps.
Check error counters on the interface.
For fiber, compare transceiver readings against thresholds; for copper, run a TDR test.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Repeated up/down events on one interface within a short window, with timestamps.
CRC, input error and output drop counters that increase.
SymbolErr frames (a Layer 1 issue), Collision fragments (suggests half-duplex), FcsErr frames (collisions, duplex mismatch or bad hardware).
Number of LinkDownEvents, last flap timestamp and last link-down/up durations.
Transceiver PID, serial and alarm/warning thresholds to compare against the datasheet.
Temperature, voltage, current and Tx/Rx power against thresholds (fiber/DOM only).

diagnostic_commands.command: test cable-diagnostics tdr, then show cable-diagnostics tdr
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: OPEN, SHORT or Impedance Mismatch per pair (copper only).
Flap count allowed before the port is placed in errdisable.

remediation: Swap the suspect cable with a known-good cable and check for broken or missing pins.
Reseat cables and transceivers; bypass the patch panel if possible.
Swap the SFP with a known-good, supported SFP.
Move the cable to a known-good port.
Replace or update the endpoint device; adjust endpoint sleep settings if they cause the flap.
Reseat or replace a network module per the platform installation guide.
Configure matching FEC on both ends.
records.operational_risk: Vendor warnings: debug commands can affect a live network (use only in a lab after reproducing the issue and disable immediately after capture); do not change port configuration or port status (for example remove the cable) during a TDR test; TDR can be invalid on an Auto-MDIX port and is not intended to locate a faulty cable; use only supported optics.
verification_steps: Not stated by the vendor as a procedure. Indirect checks in the document: no new up/down entries in show logging, and after clear counters the error counters stop incrementing.

records.symptom: A BGP neighbor session drops or does not come up (state Idle or Active).
signatures: %BGP-5-ADJCHANGE: neighbor <ip> passive Down AFI/SAFI not supported
records.meaning: The BGP session with the neighbor went down; the text after Down gives the reason (for example Interface flap, or AFI/SAFI not supported when the address families do not match).
likely_causes: Interface flap: a physical problem on the port, SFP, cable, or a disconnection.
AFI/SAFI not supported: the peers' address families do not match.
Wrong peer IP or AS configuration, or a duplicate BGP router ID.
No route to the peer, or TCP port 179 blocked by an ACL or firewall.
Authentication (MD5) mismatch.
MTU inconsistent along the path.
Control-plane overload that drops keepalives.
alternative_causes: For loopback peering: missing update-source (iBGP) or disable-connected-check / ebgp-multihop (eBGP).
Next hop unreachable, so routes are not installed (see show ip bgp rib-failure).
diagnostic_steps: Read the reason text in the ADJCHANGE message.
Check session state and prefix count, then reachability to the peer and TCP 179.
Check interface errors, MTU and control-plane CPU.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: State/PfxRcd shows a prefix count when the session is up; Idle or Active means the session is down.
A route to the peer; a missing route points to a reachability problem.
Notifications such as a wrong-AS message or a duplicate BGP identifier.
Packets reach the far end if the connection opens, is closed or refused; destination unreachable points to ACLs, firewalls or packet loss.
Input errors and input queue drops.
Identifies BGP Router, BGP Scanner, BGP I/O, BGP Open or BGP Event as the CPU consumer.
Whether the MTU is valid along the path.
Why a route did not install in the RIB.

remediation: Correct the peer IP or AS configuration on both ends; set a unique router ID with bgp router-id.
For iBGP over loopbacks define the source with neighbor <ip> update-source.
For eBGP over loopbacks between directly connected routers use neighbor <ip> disable-connected-check; for multihop eBGP use neighbor <ip> ebgp-multihop [hop-count].
Fix Layer 1 problems and review ACLs and firewalls that block TCP 179; make MTU consistent across the path.
For an address-family mismatch align the configured address families or use neighbor <ip> dont-capability-negotiate on both ends.
For next-hop problems advertise the next hop through an IGP or static route, or use neighbor <ip> next-hop-self on the iBGP peer.
records.operational_risk: Vendor: understand the impact of any command on a live network; soft-reconfiguration inbound can use about half of the BGP Local RIB table's memory, so avoid it unless required. The document states no risk for dont-capability-negotiate, disable-connected-check or weight changes (not stated).
verification_steps: show ip bgp all summary shows the neighbor up with a prefix count; after clear ip bgp <peer> soft, a prefix whose next hop is now reachable is installed and marked best.
An explicit Established-state check is not stated by the document.

records.symptom: An OSPF neighbor stays in EXSTART or EXCHANGE and never reaches FULL.
records.meaning: The two routers cannot complete database-descriptor (DBD) exchange, so the adjacency does not form.
likely_causes: MTU mismatch (the document calls this the most common cause): a router sends a DBD packet larger than the neighbor's MTU and the neighbor ignores it.
Broken unicast between the routers (wrong VC mapping in ATM/Frame Relay, an MTU limit on packet size, an access list blocking the unicast packet, or NAT translating it).
Duplicate router ID from misconfiguration.
alternative_causes: Neighbor between a PRI and a BRI/dialer interface.
RFC 2328 section 10.3 events: unexpected DD sequence number, unexpected I bit, changed option field, or BadLSReq.
diagnostic_steps: Check the neighbor state on both routers.
Watch the adjacency process for DBD retransmissions and MTU messages.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: One router shows EXCHANGE and the neighbor shows EXSTART when stuck; the document shows no healthy output.
Hellos, DBD exchange and retransmissions; messages such as 'Nbr <ip> has larger interface MTU'. Debug caution applies on live networks.

remediation: Change either router's MTU so it matches the neighbor's MTU (the document's stated solution).

ip ospf mtu-ignore on the interface turns off MTU mismatch detection; the document says it is only needed in rare instances (example: a Catalyst 5000 RSM VLAN interface with MTU 1500 facing an FDDI interface with MTU 4500).
records.operational_risk: The document states that without a fix the routers cannot leave exstart/exchange, so the adjacency never forms. Risks of ip ospf mtu-ignore are not stated.
verification_steps: Not stated by the document (no FULL-state output or verification procedure is shown).

records.symptom: A switch port is placed in err-disabled state and stops forwarding.
signatures: %PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: <cause> error detected on <interface>, putting <interface> in err-disable state
records.meaning: The port manager detected a misconfiguration or misbehavior (for example link-flap, loopback or bpduguard) and disabled the port.
likely_causes: Duplex mismatch; port-channel misconfiguration; BPDU guard violation; UDLD condition (also if UDLD is enabled on only one end).
Late-collision or link-flap detection; PAgP flap; L2TP guard; security violation; DHCP snooping rate limit; ARP inspection; inline power.
Incorrect GBIC/SFP module or cable; loopback errors.
alternative_causes: 802.1X security violations are also covered by the document.
diagnostic_steps: Identify which ports are err-disabled and the detected cause from the log.
Check recovery and detection settings and flap thresholds.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Status shows err-disabled.
The %PM-4-ERR_DISABLE message naming the cause and port.
Recovery status per cause, the timer interval and interfaces due for the next re-enable attempt.
Detection settings (the document is inconsistent about whether it also shows the reason).
Flap thresholds (example in the document: link-flap is 5 flaps in 10 seconds).

remediation: Fix the root cause first (for example match duplex on both ends, set EtherChannel to desirable mode, remove PortFast/BPDU Guard from switch-facing ports).
Manual recovery: in interface configuration mode run shutdown, then no shutdown.
Automatic recovery is disabled by default: errdisable recovery cause <cause> (or all); the default interval is 300 seconds and can be changed with errdisable recovery interval <seconds>.
records.operational_risk: Vendor: if the port is re-enabled before the root problem is fixed it becomes err-disabled again; spantree PortFast can only be enabled on ports connected to a single host (other switching devices can cause temporary loops); disable a detection cause only after assessing the loss of the protective response; understand the impact of any command on a live network.
verification_steps: show interfaces <interface> status confirms the port is no longer err-disabled.
show errdisable recovery confirms recovery settings and candidates; show etherchannel summary confirms EtherChannel status after changes.

records.symptom: An IPsec tunnel does not establish; IKE negotiation fails.
records.meaning: IKE debug output identifies where negotiation fails; 'SA proposal chosen, matched gateway' is the article's success indicator.

Tunnel bound to a loopback or internal interface without an inbound firewall policy from the WAN interface allowing IKE messages.
diagnostic_steps: Clear the IKE log filter, filter to the remote peer, enable IKE debug, reproduce the negotiation and read the output.

records.symptom: A VM processed by Veeam shows a warning that consolidation is needed and consolidation fails, or has orphaned snapshots that are not in VMware Snapshot Manager.
signatures: orphaned snapshots not shown in Snapshot Manager
records.meaning: A disk of the processed VM may remain attached to a VMware backup proxy after a HOTADD backup, preventing consolidation.
likely_causes: VMware does not process the command to release the VM's disk from the proxy.
The Veeam Backup Server crashed while processing a VM.
Jobs were forced to stop.
A backup or replication job created a snapshot on a proxy while another job was using that proxy.
alternative_causes: For a Windows-based VMware backup proxy that repeatedly gets stuck HOTADDed disks, the article says automount may not be disabled at the OS level (see KB1882).

In the vSphere Client find VMs with the consolidation warning and attempt consolidation; note which still fail.
Review each VMware backup proxy's settings for disks whose VMDK name does not match the proxy and matches an affected VM, with Disk Mode Independent - NonPersistent.

records.symptom: DNS records go missing from a DNS zone.
signatures: Netlogon "event ID 577x" when SRV records cannot be registered
records.meaning: Records disappear from a zone; Microsoft names scavenging as the most common cause.
likely_causes: DNS scavenging is misconfigured: Windows computers re-register records every 24 hours, so no-refresh and refresh intervals both below 24 hours lose records.
The host "A" record is deleted when a client changes its DNS server IP in an Active Directory-integrated zone (a deletion request to the old server replicates to the new one).
DHCP clients with ISATAP or 6to4 adapters that use DHCP Option 81 can unregister the "A" record while registering the "AAAA" record.
A DNS dynamic update to existing records fails, so scavenging treats the records as aged and deletes them.
alternative_causes: Converting an active dynamic lease to a reservation deletes the "A" and PTR records by design; they are refreshed at the next DHCP renewal.
diagnostic_steps: Check the zone aging/scavenging no-refresh and refresh intervals.
Check System event logs on the DNS servers, the affected computers and DHCP servers for registration failures (Netlogon logs 577x events for SRV registration failures).

diagnostic_commands.command: Review zone aging properties (no-refresh and refresh intervals)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Both intervals below 24 hours indicate records are being scavenged.

diagnostic_commands.command: Event Viewer: System log on DNS servers and the affected computers
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Netlogon "event ID 577x" and registration-failure events for host A and PTR records give insight into why updates failed.

remediation: Correct misconfigured scavenging intervals (vendor points to its aging and scavenging article).
For the Option 81 / ISATAP / 6to4 case, avoid configuring those DHCP clients to update DNS dynamically when DHCP servers already do so (vendor workaround).
records.operational_risk: Not stated by the vendor page. Inference: changing scavenging or dynamic-update behavior affects every record in the zone, so scope the change.
verification_steps: Not stated by the vendor. Inference: the missing records are present again after the next registration or DHCP renewal and are not removed by the next scavenging cycle.

records.symptom: DHCP clients cannot obtain an IP address lease.
records.meaning: Either the DHCP server/scope is not able to lease, or DHCP packets are dropped between client and server.
likely_causes: DHCP Server service not running or server not authorized.
No free leases in the scope, BAD_ADDRESS entries, or static IPs not excluded from the scope.
Server bound to an address outside the scope subnet (no relay agent), or another process occupying UDP 67/68.
IPsec exemption missing, or relay agent (IP helper) not configured on routers/VLAN switches.
Intermediate features such as VRRP/HSRP, Dynamic ARP Inspection or DHCP snooping.
Client side: cable, MAC filtering on the switch, disabled adapter, driver, DHCP Client service stopped, firewall blocking UDP 67/68.
alternative_causes: Network drops between client and server, identified from captures.
diagnostic_steps: Collect the vendor checklist answers (when it started, which clients/scopes, same subnet or relayed, split-scope or failover).
Check the System and DHCP-Server event channels and the DHCP server debug log (default %windir%\System32\Dhcp).
Capture on both client and server and compare DORA packets.

diagnostic_commands.command: net start (look for DHCP Server / DHCP Client)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Service is running.
The bound IP address is within the subnet of the scopes that must be leased (when no relay agent exists).
Only the DHCP server listens on UDP 67 and 68; WDS or PXE must not occupy them.

diagnostic_commands.command: DHCP management console: scope statistics and Address Leases
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Free leases exist; BAD_ADDRESS listings are noted.

diagnostic_commands.command: Wireshark on client and server; display filter dhcp (client) and dhcp.id == <Transaction ID> (server); trigger with ipconfig /renew
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: All four packets DISCOVER, OFFER, REQUEST, ACK present means DORA is likely successful; missing packets show where they are dropped (for example DISCOVER on client but not on server).

remediation: Fix the identified server, scope, relay or client setting (vendor checklist).
After drops are confirmed, involve the network team to investigate and resolve the drop (vendor step).
records.operational_risk: Not stated by the vendor page beyond running Wireshark as administrator on both devices. Changes to scopes or authorization affect all clients of the scope (inference).
verification_steps: Vendor method: repeat the capture and confirm all four DORA packets appear. Other verification is not stated.

signatures: Event ID 1721 when connecting as cluster administrator

cluster log: sponsor node is not available
records.meaning: The node cannot communicate with the cluster or cannot start ClusSvc because of blocked ports, security policy, network or configuration problems.
likely_causes: Required ports blocked by firewalls: 135 (RPC endpoint mapper, TCP and UDP), 3343 (cluster network driver), 445, 139, 5000-5099 (RPC, at least 100 ports needed), 8011-8031 (internode RPC across firewalls).
User-rights policy problems: cluster accounts missing from access-from-network / log-on-locally lists, local accounts or Everyone included in deny lists.
Group Policy "Allow Custom SSPs and APs to be loaded into LSASS" set to Disabled makes ClusSvc fail with Event 7024.
Network adapter, cabling, teaming, hub/switch/bridge problems on the cluster networks.
alternative_causes: Failed or warning results in the cluster validation report.
diagnostic_steps: Check firewall ports.
Run cluster validation.
Check security policies.
Temporarily disable the firewall between the node and the cluster to test.
Check network hardware and review cluster logs.

diagnostic_commands.command: Failover Cluster Manager (CluAdmin.msc) > Validate Configuration > Run all tests
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Review tests labelled Failed or Warning; report is in C:\Windows\Cluster\Reports (.MHT, .HTM in Windows Server 2016 and later).
Fresh cluster log; errors that a sponsor node is not available indicate missing RPC ports 8011-8031.
Cluster API Debug Tracing logs.

diagnostic_commands.command: logman create trace "base_cluster" ... -p "Microsoft-Windows-FailoverClustering-Client" ...; reproduce; logman stop base_cluster.etl -ets; netsh trace convert base_cluster.etl; Get-ClusterLog
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: More detailed trace converted into a cluster log (full command line is in the article).

Correct the user-rights lists, then try bringing the node online again.

records.symptom: VMware backup, replication or restore in Virtual appliance (HotAdd) mode fails or cannot use that mode.
signatures: Virtual appliance mode unavailable for the processed VM
records.meaning: The documentation lists requirements and limitations for the Virtual appliance mode; a proxy or VM that does not meet them cannot use it.
likely_causes: The proxy role is not assigned to a VM, or the proxy and the processed VM are not in the same datacenter.
The proxy cannot access the disks of the processed VM (for replication the source proxy needs the source disks and the target proxy the replica disks).
Latest VMware Tools is not installed on the proxy (or on a backup server acting as proxy).
A SCSI 0:X controller is not present on the proxy (documentation: VM data processing in Virtual appliance mode will fail).

Unsupported disk or storage combinations: IDE disks; source VM with vSAN disks while the proxy has non-vSAN disks (vSphere 6.5 and later); a proxy on a VMFS 3 datastore with too small a block size for the largest hot-added disk.
NFS 3.0 datastores require the proxy on the same host as the VMs (documented issue with a VMware KB and a Veeam KB).
Veeam Software Appliance: adding a local, iSCSI or FC storage device in Veeam Host Management Console restarts the HotAdd service, so HotAdd jobs and restores fail while it restarts.
alternative_causes: For Quick Migration during Instant Recovery the mode cannot be used if the proxy and the mount server or repository holding the backup are the same VM.
diagnostic_steps: Compare the proxy and the processed VM against the requirement list.
Check which transport mode the proxy is configured to use.

diagnostic_commands.command: Veeam console: Backup Infrastructure > Backup Proxies > proxy settings (transport mode)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Transport mode is manual or automatic; if Virtual appliance cannot be used the proxy can fail over to network mode only if that was configured when the proxy was added.

remediation: Meet the requirements: assign the proxy role to a VM in the same datacenter with access to the VM disks, install the latest VMware Tools, ensure a SCSI 0:X controller exists.
For NFS 3.0, place the proxy on the same host as the VMs as the documentation describes (or use ESXi 6.0 or later with NFS 4.1).
On Veeam Software Appliance, wait for HotAdd jobs and restores to complete before adding a storage device.

verification_steps: Not stated by the documentation. Inference: the previously failing job or restore completes using the Virtual appliance mode.

records.symptom: A backup job finishes with Error status after the backup file health check detects corruption, or subsequent incremental sessions end with Error.
signatures: backup job completed with Error status after health check
records.meaning: The periodic health check recomputes CRC (metadata) and hash (VM data blocks) values for the latest restore point and compares them with stored values.
likely_causes: Corrupted metadata in the full backup file: the chain from that full point is marked corrupted.
Corrupted metadata in an incremental file: that and subsequent incremental restore points are removed from the configuration database.
Corrupted VM disk blocks: the restore point with the corrupted blocks and subsequent incrementals are marked corrupted.
alternative_causes: Health check did not complete before the next schedule (the session stops and a new one starts), or jobs/restores/synthetic operations were running (the health check does not run until they finish).
diagnostic_steps: Look at the job sessions: the job completes with Error and a separate health check retry session starts.
Check the health check settings (Perform backup files health check option and schedule; default 5:00 on the last Saturday of every month).

diagnostic_commands.command: Backup job settings: Perform backup files health check option and schedule
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Enabled option and the configured schedule.

diagnostic_commands.command: Job session list / restore point state
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: The retry runs as a separate backup job session; corrupted restore points are marked in the configuration database.

remediation: Let the health check retry run: for corrupted full metadata it transports the whole VM image and creates a new full backup file; for incremental metadata corruption it creates a new incremental relative to the latest valid restore point; for corrupted data blocks it transports them again from the source.
Linux immutable repositories do not support repair: after corruption is detected, perform an active full backup for the chain, otherwise subsequent incremental sessions finish with Error status.
records.operational_risk: Documented: the health check may take long because several files of the chain must be read; for network or deduplicating storage it runs on the gateway server (place it close to the repository); encrypted files pass encryption keys to the repository. An active full backup reads the whole VM from the source (load and time are not quantified by the page). Do not delete backup files manually to fix this (see the backup-chain record).
verification_steps: Documentation: when no corruption is detected the backup job session completes in a regular way. For a retry, confirm the retry session succeeds and the latest restore point is no longer marked corrupted (inference).

signatures: capacity tier health check completes with an error
records.meaning: The capacity-tier health check verifies metadata for the whole backup and that data blocks exist on capacity extents (it lists blocks, it does not read them).
likely_causes: Corrupted metadata: the whole backup chain is marked corrupted; restore from that chain is not possible and all offload sessions for it are prevented.
Missing data blocks: those blocks and the restore points that use them are marked corrupted and are re-uploaded during the offload session.
alternative_causes: Immutable data of removed restore points can remain in the repository; the health check covers only valid restore points per the retention policy.
diagnostic_steps: View the health check result in the restore point statistics (it lists corrupted data and the restore points sharing the corrupted blocks).
Check the health check schedule in the scale-out repository settings (default: monthly, last Saturday, during the offload session after backup cleanup).

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Corrupted data and all restore points that share the corrupted data blocks.

remediation: Missing blocks: Veeam re-uploads them to the capacity extent during the next offload session (documented behavior).
Corrupted metadata: to add a new backup chain to the capacity tier you must delete the corrupted chain from the capacity tier or detach the backup from the backup job (documented).
records.operational_risk: Documented: with corrupted metadata you cannot restore from that chain. Deleting the corrupted chain or detaching the backup is destructive/irreversible for that chain; do it only with a verified recovery plan (inference from the documented consequence).
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: after re-upload the restore points are no longer marked corrupted and the next offload session completes.

records.symptom: A scheduled synthetic full or active full backup is not created on the expected day.
signatures: no full backup created on the scheduled day
records.meaning: Several scheduling conditions suppress a scheduled full backup.
likely_causes: Synthetic and active full backups both enabled and scheduled on the same day: the synthetic full is not created.
A job chained after an initial job, where the initial job does not run on the day the full backup is scheduled: no full backup is created.
Active full: the parent backup job is not scheduled to run automatically or is disabled.
Synthetic full for backup jobs targeting object storage cannot be created independently: GFS policy must be enabled.
The Create synthetic full backups periodically on option is not enabled or no days are scheduled.
alternative_causes: A regular session scheduled the same day as an active full produces only the active full; the incremental that would have been added is not created (documented, not an error).
diagnostic_steps: Compare the job schedule and settings with the documented conditions.

diagnostic_commands.command: Backup job Advanced Settings: full backup schedule
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Synthetic full option enabled with scheduled days; active full schedule present; parent job enabled and scheduled.

remediation: Adjust the schedule so the conflicting conditions do not apply (different days, run the initial job on the chained job full-backup day, enable the job, enable GFS for object storage synthetic fulls).
records.operational_risk: Not stated by the documentation. Full backups reset the backup chain; an active full reads the whole VM from the source, a synthetic full consolidates existing repository files (documented descriptions).
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: a full backup file appears in the repository on the next scheduled day.

records.symptom: An expected OSPF neighbor is missing from the neighbor table, shows Down, or is stuck in Init.
signatures: show ip ospf neighbor shows no entry, DOWN or INIT
records.meaning: No valid HELLOs are received (no state), HELLOs stopped within the Dead interval (Down), or HELLOs arrive without the local Router ID in the neighbor field (Init, no two-way).
likely_causes: No state: interface or line protocol down; no IP reachability; ACL or switch blocking; OSPF not enabled or interface passive; duplicate Router IDs; mismatched area, area type, subnet/mask or Hello/Dead timers; crossed parallel point-to-point links; OSPF only on a secondary network; high CPU/memory; Layer 1/2 fault.
Down: neighbor router down, inactive, or not configured for OSPF on that interface.
Init: the local Router ID does not appear in the neighbor Hello (page gives no further cause).
alternative_causes: Exstart/Exchange is covered by the EXSTART record (MTU mismatch, DBD sequence number).
Loading: corrupted LSAs, indicated by %OSPF-4-BADLSA; the page says to contact Cisco TAC and gives no commands.
diagnostic_steps: Confirm interface and line protocol, then IP reachability, then OSPF interface settings, Router ID and neighbor identity.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Neighbor state (DOWN, INIT, 2-WAY, EXSTART/EXCHANGE, LOADING, FULL).
Interface and line protocol up; IP subnet and MTU.
Neighbor responds; traceroute shows no more than one hop; the OSPF multicast address answers.
Timers, network type and passive status; an active interface shows "Hello due in"; passive interfaces send no HELLOs.
Router ID (must be unique) and area/stub settings.
Neighbor name and PortID match the design (point-to-point links).

diagnostic_commands.command: show memory summary; show memory processor
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Memory/resource problems that can block HELLO processing.
Adjacency formation. The page says to use debug with caution.

remediation: Correct the mismatched parameter on the interface (the page names no verbatim command for most causes; it says to make the mismatched parameters match).

For manually configured neighbors on NBMA use neighbor with ip ospf network non-broadcast, or ip ospf network point-to-multipoint non-broadcast (the neighbor command works only for directly attached neighbors on those network types).
If the checks pass and no state appears, the page says to contact Cisco TAC.
records.operational_risk: Page warnings: debug commands should be used with caution; OSPF adjacencies form only over primary networks, not secondary networks. Other risks are not stated.
verification_steps: The page defines the healthy end state: show ip ospf neighbor shows FULL ("synchronized views on a link-state database").

official_sources.scope: Neighbor states, causes, checks and corrective actions.

records.version_scope: Veeam Backup & Replication 13 documentation, build 13.1.2.57 (page updated 2026-04-24).
records.symptom: Instant Recovery fails, the recovered VM does not boot, or the vPower NFS datastore runs out of space.
signatures: restore will fail (vVol or ESXi 8.0 case)
recovered Linux VM does not boot
records.meaning: The documentation lists preconditions and limits for Instant Recovery; violating them causes failure or an unbootable VM.
likely_causes: No successfully created restore point in the backup.

Not enough free space in the vPower NFS datastore: minimum free space equals the RAM of the recovered VM plus 200 MB (Quick Migration with Smart Switch needs additional free space equal to the RAM of the recovered VM), and usage grows with write activity (default location: the IRCache folder on the volume with most free space).

vSphere 8.0 and later: the backed-up VM has disks on a vVol datastore or is located on an ESXi 8.0+ host (documented: restore will fail); a vVol datastore cannot be the destination for virtual disk updates.
Linux workloads without dracut, mkinitrd or initramfs, or with filesystems mounted by block device name instead of UUID in /etc/fstab: the restored VM may not boot.
Original workload still powered on when restoring to the production network (documented: make sure it is powered off).
Unsupported items: BSD operating systems, Cluster Shared Volumes (cluster disks used as CSV are excluded), 4K native drives for Veeam Agents.
alternative_causes: Redirecting virtual disk updates to a vSphere datastore means the vPower NFS datastore is not used.
diagnostic_steps: Check the restore point exists and is successful.
Check free space in the vPower NFS datastore (IRCache) against RAM + 200 MB.
Check vVol/ESXi version conditions and, for Linux, initramfs tooling and /etc/fstab UUIDs.

diagnostic_commands.command: Backup Infrastructure: vPower NFS datastore volume free space (default C:\ProgramData\Veeam\Backup\IRCache)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Free space at least the recovered VM RAM plus 200 MB.
All filesystems mounted by UUID.

remediation: Provide enough free space or redirect virtual disk updates to a vSphere datastore (not vVol).
Install dracut, mkinitrd or initramfs on Linux workloads before backup; mount filesystems by UUID.
Power off the original workload before recovering to the production network.
records.operational_risk: Documented: the actual vPower NFS space usage grows during the session with write activity. Data-loss risk is not stated; recovery to the production network with the original powered on is documented as something to avoid (duplicate workload).
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: the recovered VM boots and its disk updates are finalized or migrated before the Instant Recovery session is stopped.

official_sources.scope: Prerequisites and limitations for Instant Recovery.

records.symptom: A SureBackup job fails to verify a machine, or the session is marked Failed.
records.meaning: SureBackup starts machines from backups in an isolated virtual lab and runs heartbeat, ping and application tests, then optionally validates backup files with a CRC check.
likely_causes: Verification tests (heartbeat, ping, application, custom scripts) fail for the machine under verification or the application group.
Backup file validation fails: if verification tests succeed but the CRC/checksum validation does not pass, the session is marked Failed.
Boot time or application initialization limits are too short (the page names Maximum allowed boot time and Application initialization timeout as values to inspect).
alternative_causes: If a machine has multiple partitions with different operating systems, only the partition with the highest boot priority is verified.
Internal connectivity problems inside the virtual lab.
diagnostic_steps: Start the failed VM in troubleshooting mode to investigate.

diagnostic_commands.command: Veeam console: Home > Jobs > SureBackup > right-click job > Statistics > right-click the failed VM > Start (troubleshooting mode)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: The VM and application group stay powered on until stopped manually, so lab connectivity and the boot/initialization timeouts can be inspected.

remediation: Use troubleshooting mode to diagnose lab connectivity and adjust Maximum allowed boot time and Application initialization timeout. Stop the session from the Session Statistics window or by stopping the job.
records.operational_risk: Documented: troubleshooting mode keeps the VM and application group powered on until you stop it manually, and powers the application group on again if it was off. During verification the backed-up image stays read-only; changes go to redo logs (VMware) or a differencing disk (Hyper-V) that are discarded afterwards.
verification_steps: Re-run the SureBackup job and confirm the session no longer shows Failed (inference); the CRC validation runs after all live tests and decides the session state.

records.symptom: Application-aware processing fails or cannot be used for a VM; backups are only crash-consistent.
signatures: no VSS writer for the application
records.meaning: By default Veeam creates crash-consistent backups; application-aware processing must be enabled and the guest must meet requirements.
likely_causes: VMware Tools or the latest guest updates are not installed.
Unsupported guest OS (supported: Linux-based VMs, Windows client from Vista, Windows Server from 2012 R2 SP1).
A gMSA is used for application-aware processing of SharePoint or PostgreSQL (not supported).
The application has no Microsoft VSS writer (the page gives MySQL as an example), so VSS-based processing cannot be used.

The account lacks the required rights: for Windows guests Logon as a batch job granted and Deny logon as a batch job not set (gMSAs also Logon as a service); application-specific rights such as local Administrator plus SQL Server sysadmin or the listed minimal roles.
Oracle on Linux: /tmp not mounted with the exec option gives a permission denial error.
alternative_causes: Application-aware processing for Active Directory, SQL Server, SharePoint, Exchange, Oracle and PostgreSQL must be enabled in job settings to get transactionally consistent backups.
diagnostic_steps: Check guest OS version, VMware Tools and updates; check the guest processing account rights; check whether a VSS writer exists for the application.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Application-aware processing enabled with an account that meets the listed rights.

remediation: Install VMware Tools and updates; use a supported account type; grant the listed permissions.
For applications without a VSS writer use VMware Tools quiescence with pre-freeze and post-thaw scripts (vendor alternative).
For Oracle on Linux mount /tmp with exec.
records.operational_risk: Not stated beyond the requirements. Granting Local Administrator or sysadmin rights to the guest processing account is a security-sensitive change (inference): prefer the documented minimal permissions.
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: the job session shows application-aware processing succeeded and, if configured, log truncation or log backup completes.

records.symptom: A backup job to a scale-out repository fails or restores are blocked after an extent was put into Maintenance mode.
signatures: backup job targeted at the scale-out repository fails
records.meaning: Maintenance mode restricts data transfer to the extent and blocks restore of data on it and of chains that partly reside on it.

records.symptom: Both units of an ASA/FTD failover pair are Active (split-brain) and traffic is disrupted.
signatures: show failover state: both units Active, peer Failed with reason Comm Failure
records.meaning: The units cannot detect each other and both take the active role, so both use the same interface IP and MAC addresses and the upstream switch MAC table can be inconsistent.
likely_causes: Failover link down, unidirectionally or bidirectionally.
Layer 1 faults: faulty cable, SFP or interface.
A problem on an intermediate device.
Memory or CPU exhaustion; depletion of the 1550-byte block pool can stop failover packet processing.
alternative_causes: Not stated beyond the listed causes.
diagnostic_steps: Run the state command on both units, check the failover link and Layer 1, check block depletion, and check which unit the upstream MAC table points to.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Split-brain: both boxes show Active and the other host shows Failed with Comm Failure.
Depletion of the 1550-byte block pool (possible cause).
Healthy: separate active and standby MACs on different ports; the active MACs for the data interfaces should all point to a single unit.
Data to send to Cisco TAC with topology, syslogs from about 5 minutes before and after, and FXOS files for Firepower hardware.

remediation: Emergency recovery (vendor): disable failover on the unit that is not passing traffic (ASA: no failover in configuration mode; FTD: configure high-availability suspend from Clish).
Isolate that unit from the network (ASA: shut the data interfaces; FTD: shut the interfaces on the connected device; or physically disconnect or power off).

If connectivity problems persist, clear stale ARP entries on upstream and downstream devices, or force the working unit to send a gratuitous ARP for the affected interface IP with debug menu ipaddrutl 6 <interface ip address> (from system support diagnostics-cli on FTD).

Prevention listed by the vendor: Cisco-recommended release, separate paths for data and failover links, port-channel for the failover link, link latency under 10 ms (no more than 250 ms), hold timer five times the poll timer, virtual MAC addresses, logs from both units to an external syslog server.
records.operational_risk: Vendor warnings: disabling failover or isolating a unit interrupts service on that unit and removes redundancy until failover is restored; powering off limits management access; changing the active unit can cause stale ARP entries and traffic disruption; without virtual MAC addresses the ARP tables on connected routers must be cleared; the unit cannot fail over while the failover link is down, so restore the link as soon as possible.
verification_steps: The page gives no dedicated verification command. Its recovery goal: only one unit is Active in show failover state, the MAC addresses learned for the active IPs point to a single unit, and traffic flows normally.

records.symptom: A repository cannot be added as a scale-out repository extent, a job cannot target the scale-out repository, or jobs fail because of extent-count limits.
signatures: jobs targeted at the scale-out repository fail (4 performance extents, none in Maintenance mode)
records.meaning: The documentation lists job types and repository states that cannot be used with a scale-out backup repository, and edition-based extent limits.
likely_causes: Jobs of unsupported types target the repository or its data (for example replica metadata): configuration backup, replication (including seeding), VM copy for VMware, file backup and object storage backup jobs for object-storage extents.

The repository is already an extent of another scale-out repository, is used by VMware Cloud Director organizations, is a Cloud Connect cloud repository, or has an activity (backup job or restore) running.
A scale-out repository cannot be added as an extent of another one; once a repository is an extent you must target jobs to the scale-out repository, not to the extent.

alternative_causes: More than 24 active extents in one tier is not recommended (performance issues).

diagnostic_commands.command: Veeam console: Backup Infrastructure view (Scale-out Repositories node)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Extent membership and the jobs targeting each repository.

remediation: Target unsupported jobs to another repository and remove that job data from the repository before adding it as an extent (vendor step).
Put an extent into Maintenance mode where the edition limit requires an inactive extent; use Veeam Universal License or Enterprise Plus for no extent-count limit (documented).
records.operational_risk: Removing job data from a repository is destructive for that data; do not remove replica metadata or other job data without a verified recovery plan (inference).
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: the repository is accepted as an extent and jobs targeted at the scale-out repository run.

records.symptom: A transaction is aborted with a deadlock error while other transactions complete.
records.meaning: Two or more transactions each hold locks the other wants; PostgreSQL detects the situation automatically and aborts one transaction (which one is hard to predict).
likely_causes: Transactions acquire locks on multiple objects in inconsistent order (documented example: two transactions updating the same two rows in opposite order; row-level locks can deadlock without explicit locking).
The first lock taken on an object is not the most restrictive mode later needed (documented advice).
Transactions held open for long periods (for example while waiting for user input), because a waiter waits indefinitely until a deadlock is detected.
alternative_causes: The deadlock check runs only after deadlock_timeout (default 1 s); raising it slows reporting of real deadlocks.
diagnostic_steps: Identify the statements and rows involved from the server log (log_lock_waits reports waits longer than deadlock_timeout).
Review the order in which the applications lock multiple objects.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: A log message once a session has waited longer than deadlock_timeout for a lock; the deadlock error itself identifies the aborted transaction.
Current wait before the deadlock check (default 1s).

remediation: Make every application acquire locks on multiple objects in a consistent order; take the most restrictive needed lock mode first (documented best defense).
If that is not feasible in advance, retry transactions that abort due to deadlocks (documented).
Avoid holding transactions open for long periods.
records.operational_risk: Documented: which transaction is aborted should not be relied upon; the aborted transaction must be retried by the application. Changing deadlock_timeout trades reporting delay against needless checks (documented); the page gives no data-loss risk beyond the aborted transaction.
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: the deadlock error no longer recurs for the same statements and retries succeed.

records.symptom: WAL archiving keeps failing and the pg_wal directory keeps growing.
signatures: archive command returns a nonzero status
records.meaning: A nonzero archive_command/archive_library result tells PostgreSQL the file was not archived; it retries periodically and meanwhile pg_wal keeps filling with WAL segments.
likely_causes: The archive command or library fails repeatedly because something needs operator intervention or the archive runs out of space (example: a tape that is full).
The archive command returns a wrong status (it must return zero if and only if it succeeds, and a nonzero status when a different file with the same name already exists).
alternative_causes: If the archive command is terminated by a signal other than SIGTERM, or by a shell error such as command not found, archiving is treated as an error (documented).
diagnostic_steps: Check the archive destination and the exit status behavior of the command; check free space on the file system containing pg_wal.

diagnostic_commands.command: Server log: messages about the failing archive command
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Repeated failures for the same WAL segment file (the page says the server retries periodically).

diagnostic_commands.command: Free space on the file system containing pg_wal
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Shrinking free space while archiving is failing.

remediation: Resolve the archive error (free archive space, fix the command or its exit status) so archiving resumes; make sure error conditions are reported to an operator (documented).
records.operational_risk: Documented: if the file system containing pg_wal fills up, PostgreSQL does a PANIC shutdown; no committed transactions are lost but the database stays offline until space is freed. records.symptom: Queries on a hot standby are canceled (or a session is terminated) because they conflict with WAL replay.
records.meaning: The standby cannot fail to apply WAL already applied on the primary, so after max_standby_archive_delay / max_standby_streaming_delay it cancels conflicting queries.
likely_causes: Access Exclusive locks on the primary (explicit LOCK and DDL) conflicting with standby queries.
Early cleanup: VACUUM removes row versions still visible to a standby transaction (the most common cause), or sets a page all-visible against a standby query that disagrees.
Dropping a tablespace or a database on the primary while the standby uses it (replaying DROP DATABASE terminates the whole session).
A conflict over a lock held by an idle transaction terminates that session (documented, may change).
alternative_causes: A heavy update load or long queries make the standby fall behind (documented).
diagnostic_steps: Check the cancellation counts and reasons on the standby, and the delay settings.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Number of query cancels and the reason for them.
Summary conflict information.
Whether a log message is produced when WAL replay waits longer than deadlock_timeout for conflicts.

remediation: Set hot_standby_feedback so VACUUM does not remove recently-dead rows (documented first option).
Adjust max_standby_archive_delay / max_standby_streaming_delay: short for a standby meant for high availability, higher or infinite when it runs long queries (documented trade-off).
Retry canceled queries in a new transaction (documented: they may succeed).
records.operational_risk: Documented: hot_standby_feedback delays cleanup of dead rows on the primary and may cause table bloat; a long delay setting means the standby can fall behind and long queries may not see recent changes.
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: pg_stat_database_conflicts stops growing and canceled queries succeed on retry.

records.symptom: The server logs a wraparound warning, or refuses new transaction IDs ("database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss").
signatures: WARNING: database "<db>" must be vacuumed within <N> transactions
ERROR: database is not accepting commands to avoid wraparound data loss in database "<db>"
records.meaning: Transaction IDs are 32-bit; every table must be vacuumed (rows frozen) at least once every two billion transactions or old rows would appear to be in the future. Warnings start at forty million transactions before wraparound; below three million the system refuses to assign new XIDs and only read-only transactions can start.
likely_causes: Autovacuum fails to clear old XIDs from a table.
Old prepared transactions, long-running open transactions, or old replication slots holding back the oldest XID (documented checks).
alternative_causes: A manual VACUUM run by a non-superuser fails to process system catalogs, so datfrozenxid cannot advance (documented).
diagnostic_steps: Check pg_prepared_xacts, pg_stat_activity and pg_replication_slots for old XIDs, then vacuum the target database.

diagnostic_commands.command: pg_prepared_xacts: rows where age(transactionid) is large
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Old prepared transactions to commit or roll back.

diagnostic_commands.command: pg_stat_activity: rows where age(backend_xid) or age(backend_xmin) is large
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Long-running open transactions to end.

diagnostic_commands.command: pg_replication_slots: slots where age(xmin) or age(catalog_xmin) is large
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Old slots, often for servers that no longer exist or have been down a long time.

records.symptom: The log reports checkpoints caused by filling WAL segment files happening close together.
signatures: checkpoint_warning message in the server log
records.meaning: A checkpoint starts every checkpoint_timeout (default 5 minutes) or when max_wal_size (default 1 GB) is about to be exceeded; checkpoint_warning writes a log message if size-triggered checkpoints are closer together than its value (default 30 seconds), which the vendor says suggests max_wal_size ought to be raised.

records.meaning: The documentation lists bucket/container settings that must or must not be set when Veeam manages immutability on S3, Azure Blob and Google Cloud storage.
likely_causes: Amazon S3: default retention enabled on the Object Lock bucket (it may result in unpredictable system behavior and data loss; Veeam uses Compliance mode per object).

records.symptom: An HA cluster does not form, a member keeps shutting down, or both units act as primary (split brain).
signatures: get system ha status shows each FortiGate as the primary
records.meaning: Members that cannot talk on the heartbeat interface each consider themselves primary and apply the same IP and virtual MAC addresses, causing IP/MAC conflicts and L2 flapping.
likely_causes: Complete loss of the heartbeat link(s), physically or because something blocks heartbeat packets.
Congestion and latency on heartbeat links exceeding the heartbeat lost intervals and thresholds.
Mismatched HA settings between members (mode, group-name, group-id, password).
Members that are not the same model, hardware configuration, connections and generation.

diagnostic_commands.command: get system ha status (on the console)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Healthy: HA formed with one primary; split brain: each FortiGate shows itself as primary. The page does not give healthy example output.

remediation: Restore the heartbeat link or remove what blocks heartbeat packets; make mode, group-name, group-id and password identical (different group-id values produce different virtual MACs but an IP conflict can still occur).

Prevention (vendor): use back-to-back heartbeat links in a two-member cluster, redundant heartbeat interfaces, and heartbeat lost intervals/thresholds longer than link latency for geographically separated members.

records.version_scope: Veeam Backup & Replication 13 documentation, build 13.1.2.57 (Snapshot Hunter pages updated 2025-02-10 and 2024-02-16).
records.symptom: A VM keeps snapshot files after a backup or replication session even though vSphere reported the snapshot removed ("phantom" snapshots), or consolidation is needed.
signatures: snapshot files not registered in vSphere remain on the datastore
records.meaning: vSphere can report a successful snapshot removal while the consolidation step failed (for example locked files), leaving delta files that take datastore space, hurt VM performance and can stop production VMs if the datastore fills.
likely_causes: The snapshot was removed from the list but consolidation failed, for example because files appeared locked when vSphere tried to consolidate.
alternative_causes: KB1775 describes stuck disks on a HotAdd proxy as another cause of consolidation problems.
diagnostic_steps: Check the Snapshot Hunter sessions in the History view (System) and the job statistics; check datastore free space.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Snapshot Hunter sessions; the job statistics show a warning when no consolidation attempt fit the backup window.

remediation: Veeam runs the Snapshot Hunter in every backup/replication job session: it finds orphaned snapshot files and consolidates in the background with a three-step algorithm (VMware Consolidate; hard consolidation without quiesce; hard consolidation with quiesce), up to 4 times at 4-hour intervals, then sends an email notification asking for manual troubleshooting (global email notifications must be enabled).
The two hard-consolidation steps run only when the VM has no user snapshots; VMware Cloud Director VMs are skipped.
records.operational_risk: Documented: hard consolidation creates a new snapshot and calls VMware Delete all snapshots, deleting all VM snapshots and associated files; attempts that do not fit the job backup window are not performed. Snapshots left on a full datastore can stop production VMs.
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: the VM no longer reports consolidation needed and orphaned snapshot files are gone.

records.symptom: A traffic log with subtype=local shows policyid=0 (possibly with action=accept) and it is unclear whether traffic is being denied.
records.meaning: For local traffic (traffic to or from the FortiGate itself) policy ID 0 means no user-defined local-in policy matched. The page states policy ID 0 is NOT the same as implicit deny in this context; its example shows action="accept" with policyid=0 and service="udp/520".
likely_causes: Local traffic is governed by interface Administrative Access, VPN and VIP configuration and local-in policies, not the normal firewall policies.

Only the default ports listed under Policy & Objects > Local In Policy are allowed by policy ID 0 (page example: port 443 allowed, port 4433 from the same source denied under policy ID 0; the list itself is in a screenshot).
alternative_causes: Forward-traffic implicit-deny logs also use policy ID 0 but with subtype="forward" (see the forward-traffic candidate); the two must not be conflated.
diagnostic_steps: Read subtype and action before interpreting policyid=0.
For local traffic check interface administrative access, VPN/VIP settings and local-in policies.

diagnostic_commands.command: config log setting (local-in-allow, local-in-deny-unicast, local-in-deny-broadcast, local-out)
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: The page says these local traffic logging options are disabled by default; enabling them makes local traffic logs appear.

diagnostic_commands.command: config firewall local-in-policy / local-in-policy6: set logtraffic
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Per-policy local-in logging; the page ties the new per-policy option (set local-in-policy-log under config log setting) to v7.6.X.

remediation: The page gives no remediation beyond the logging options listed; it explains that policy ID 0 is hit only when no configured local-in policy matches.
records.operational_risk: Not stated by the page. Inference: enabling local traffic logging increases log volume.
verification_steps: Not stated.

records.version_scope: Technical tip posted 2020-03-02. The page says "FortiGate" and states no FortiOS version; 6.2 is not mentioned.
records.symptom: Forward traffic is denied with policyid=0 although the administrator believes a matching firewall policy exists.
records.meaning: Forward traffic that matches no firewall policy is logged against policy ID 0 (implicit deny). The page shows the debug-flow evidence "after check: ret-no-match" followed by "Denied by forward policy check (policy 0)".
likely_causes: Default objects were modified: the address object, the schedule, or the service "ALL" no longer allows all ports.
The source or destination network/subnet does not match the address objects in the policy.
alternative_causes: Local-traffic policy ID 0 has a different meaning (see the local-traffic candidate); other causes are not covered by the page.
diagnostic_steps: Run a debug flow filtered on the source and destination IPs and ports and generate the traffic; compare the objects in the intended policy with the traffic.

diagnostic_commands.command: diagnose debug flow (filter on source/destination IP and port, then generate traffic) - exact commands are in the FortiOS 6.2.0 packet-flow candidate
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Lines "after check: ret-no-match, act-accept..." and "Denied by forward policy check (policy 0)" indicate no matching policy. The page does not give the exact commands.

remediation: Check the objects in the policy: set the service "ALL" back to its default or adjust it; the defaults named by the page are Default Service: ALL, Default Schedule: always, Default Address Object: all.
If a specific address object is used, confirm the source and destination subnets match and add the correct address objects to the policy (vendor steps).
records.operational_risk: The page states no warnings. Inference: widening objects to stop drops widens what the policy permits; scope the change narrowly.
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: the debug flow no longer reports policy 0 and the traffic matches the intended policy.

records.symptom: An HA cluster changed primary unit and the reason must be read from the HA status output.
signatures: is selected as the primary because ...
records.meaning: get sys ha status shows the last HA events and, per event, the reason the primary was selected; the article lists the documented strings.
likely_causes: Monitored interface down ("the value 0 of link-failure + pingsvr-failure is less than peer member").
Peer member down ("it's the only member in the cluster").
Override enabled and a higher-priority unit rejoined ("override priority is larger than peer member").
Override disabled and the unit with the larger uptime kept the role ("uptime is larger than peer member"), also produced by an HA uptime reset.
High memory usage on the peer ("high memory usage on peer member").
Manual failover ("EXE_FAIL_OVER flag is set on peer member", linked to execute ha failover set).
alternative_causes: Initial election by serial number ("serialno is larger than peer member") is not a failover cause.
diagnostic_steps: Run get sys ha status on any member, read the primary-selection lines with timestamps, and classify each with the documented strings.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: The failover reason and time in the "Primary selected using" lines; the FortiOS 6.2.0 Cookbook shows the same output with "Master selected using".

remediation: No remediation: the strings explain why a transition happened; address the underlying condition (interface, peer, memory, manual action) with the unexpected-failover candidate.
records.operational_risk: Not stated by the article. A transition is not necessarily a fault (override, manual failover and uptime reset are normal operations).
verification_steps: Not applicable: interpretation aid.

records.version_scope: Article published 2022-11-08, updated 2026-04-24: scope "FortiGate on High Availability clusters"; no FortiOS version stated (it links 6.0.0 and 7.6.6 documentation); FortiOS 6.2 is not mentioned.
records.symptom: The cluster fails over or transitions unexpectedly.
signatures: HA events in get system ha status
link status changes in diagnose sys ha history read
records.meaning: Monitored-interface changes, heartbeat problems, uptime/age differences and manual changes can trigger the election algorithm.
likely_causes: Monitored interface status changes (0 = down, 1 = up); a LAG/aggregate is down only when all members are down (min-links default 1); each monitored interface down at boot adds 50 to link_failure.
Uptime or link_failure differences, which trigger transitions only after the cluster has been up longer than ha-uptime-diff-margin (default 300 seconds).
A manual HA uptime reset ("Reset HA uptime"), manual HA setting changes or changes on network devices.
Heartbeat cable/port problems; WAN flapping when WAN is the only monitored interface.
alternative_causes: Not all listed conditions are faults; some are expected behavior.
diagnostic_steps: Review get system ha status, then diagnose sys ha history read (election history, limited to 512 entries), then the dump and mac outputs.

diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: Warnings near the top, the last four HA events, sync status, heartbeat interface counters and primary/secondary roles.
Election history (up to 512 entries); look for link status changes.

diagnostic_commands.command: diagnose sys ha dump-by group / dump-by vcluster
diagnostic_commands.expected_evidence: linkfails, mondev (1 = up, 0 = down), state (2 = primary, 3 = secondary), link_failure and uptime/reset_cnt.
Interface status on both members (1 = down, 0 = up).

remediation: No single fix is given: identify the trigger from the outputs, check monitored interfaces and LAG members (adjust min-links if needed), verify heartbeat cables/ports; reset uptime (diagnose sys ha reset-uptime) or health status (diagnose sys ha reset-health-status) only when appropriate.
records.operational_risk: Vendor warnings: resetting the uptime manually may cause a cluster transition; without redundant WAN links internet access can be interrupted during the impact window.
verification_steps: Not stated. Inference: no new unexpected transitions and sync status shows in-sync.
